header.incumbent: Their existing payments provider (unnamed); support was a ticket form
header.tag_why: Halima, the decider, chose on who would be named and on call during an on-sale, and our tiered support plans and response times did not answer that.

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For buyers who run live on-sales, especially an operations or COO decider: "A name, not a queue." Someone who picks up. Name the solutions engineer and account lead who will be on the account, and put in writing what happens at minute four of an on-sale and who is on call for every major on-sale. Do not lead with tiers or response times. Only publish the on-call commitment once the team confirms it can staff it.
messaging_changes.why: The decider heard our tiers and response times as "a queue with a faster timer" and wanted a person, while the winning competitor promised named people and on-call coverage for every major on-sale.

messaging_changes.change: Add a written on-sale plan as a sales asset for ticketing and live-event buyers. It shows what we do on an on-sale morning: who is named on the account, who is on call, what the shared channel is, and what happens in the first minutes of a failure. Walk the operations decider through it directly, not only the technical champion.
messaging_changes.why: The decider "wanted to see, on paper, what we do on an on-sale morning", we had no such artifact, and the rep says it could have been built with the solutions engineer.

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: For live-event and ticketing buyers: offer a conversation with a named customer who has run a real on-sale with us, instead of leading with logos or customer stories. Line: "Talk to someone who has been through an on-sale with us."
messaging_changes.why: The rep says "I had logos. I didn't have a person," and the customer asked "who," not for more proof of reliability.

messaging_changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
messaging_changes.change: For a buyer who owns the consequences of a failure, pair the technical proof with the decider's framing: "I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down." Open the COO-facing conversation on who responds when payments fail during an on-sale, and treat the load test and sandbox story as support for the engineer, not the case for the decider.
messaging_changes.why: The load test went well with the CTO, but the COO decided in one meeting and said she does not buy uptime.

trigger.insight: Payments had reportedly failed in two earlier on-sales without triggering a replacement, so the failure alone was not the trigger. CEO visibility and an unanswered support ticket during the incident were what changed. The buying problem was framed around who responds when it breaks, not around preventing the failure.
trigger.messaging: Lead with what happens in the first minutes of a live failure and who responds, instead of opening on generic reliability or growth language like M1.

competitor.insight: Everything here comes from Ben secondhand, and the competitor is never named. What is established is the shift: after that meeting the questions moved from technical to people. Jordan's view that they over-promised is an admitted guess (E15) and should not shape positioning. Whether the competitor's promise was real is unknown, and it won because it was concrete and present in the room, whether or not it was deliverable.
competitor.messaging: Counter the named-people, on-call promise with something equally concrete and specific, not with claims that competitors overpromise.

message.messaging: Retire the tiers-and-response-times framing in M5 for buyers like this and replace it with named people and a written on-sale response plan.

decided.insight: Jordan felt the loss at Halima's sentence, but calling us the favourite rests on Ben's enthusiasm, not on the decider's view, which was never shown. Jordan read the technical win as the whole deal, and the questions had already shifted to names before then (E17). The signal was there earlier than the moment Jordan names.
decided.messaging: Give reps a decider-level checklist, such as whether the person who owns the consequences has seen a plan for failure, before they call a deal favoured.

gaps.insight: The gap was not a product capability. It was a missing artifact (an on-sale plan) and a missing reference who could speak to a real on-sale, and Jordan says the plan could have been built. Whether our team could actually staff on-call on-sale coverage is not established in the transcript.
gaps.messaging: Create a reusable on-sale plan template and a ticketing reference customer, so M8 offers a person to talk to instead of logos.

language.insight: The customer described the need as a person and an event, never as support, and Halima explicitly devalued uptime, which is the core of our technical proof. Our vocabulary of plans, tiers and uptime sits on the wrong side of how she framed the problem. E34 and E36 do not name the speaker, so they may not all be Halima's words.
language.messaging: Rewrite support copy around who picks up and what happens at minute four of an on-sale, using the customer's phrases in place of tiers and plans.

gaps.question: Who was the competitor, and what is known about how they actually staffed on-sales?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan for the competitor's name and whether Ben or anyone at Tixhaven has since said whether the on-call promise was delivered.

gaps.question: Did Halima ever hear from anyone besides Ben and Jordan about our technical story, and did Jordan meet her directly beyond the support-plan session?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan and Ben how many direct touchpoints Halima had with us before her decision.

gaps.question: Why did Halima choose the competitor beyond the names and on-call promise, such as pricing or contract terms?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ben, or Halima if reachable, what in the final meeting decided it and whether cost or terms played any part.

close.rep_takeaway: You won the engineer and lost the person who owned the outcome. When the decider asks 'who's my person,' answer with a name and a written plan, not tiers. You said you could have built an on-sale plan and didn't, so next time build it as soon as the question shifts from technical to people.
